symbols.name: integer to invert
symbols.meaning: The integer whose modular inverse is sought.
symbols.quote: A modular inverse of an integer $h$, the integer to be inverted, modulo a positive integer $p$, the modulus, is an integer that undoes multiplication by $h$ up to multiples of $p$.

symbols.name: modulus
symbols.meaning: The positive integer modulus by which congruence is taken.
symbols.quote: A modular inverse of an integer $h$, the integer to be inverted, modulo a positive integer $p$, the modulus, is an integer that undoes multiplication by $h$ up to multiples of $p$.

symbols.name: modular inverse
symbols.meaning: An integer whose product with h is congruent to 1 modulo p.
symbols.quote: An integer $\mu$ is a modular inverse of $h$ modulo $p$ when $h\mu \equiv 1 \pmod p$.

symbols.name: Bézout cofactor
symbols.meaning: The integer multiplying p in the identity h\mu + p\nu = 1.
symbols.quote: When the greatest common divisor is $1$, the identity gives an integer $\mu$ and a second integer $\nu$, the cofactor that multiplies $p$, with $h\mu + p\nu = 1$.

symbols.name: group order
symbols.meaning: The number of elements of the cyclic group, which is the product of all axis lengths.
symbols.quote: Let $S$ be the product of all axis lengths, the number of elements in the cyclic group that the map targets.

relations.quote: A modular inverse is defined by a [congruence](congruence-modulo.md) modulo $p$: $h\mu$ and $1$ leave the same remainder on division by $p$, so $h\mu - 1$ is a multiple of $p$.
An inverse exists exactly when $h$ and $p$ are [coprime](coprime.md), that is, when their greatest common divisor is $1$.
Conversely, the inverse is obtained from [Bézout's identity](bezout-identity.md) applied to $h$ and $p$.
Each inverse supplies exponents for placing the [radix-digit coefficients](radix-digit-convolution.md) on cyclic axes.
Together the inverses help determine the generator of a [cyclic group](cyclic-group.md) of order $S$.
